text: Pre-existing: my open-source oneapi-agent-toolkit, the SYCL tools and agent loop, used here as a pinned dependency. Built this week: Muse Port. Meta's Muse plans and ports CUDA code against hidden checks, then tunes it on real NVIDIA and AMD GPUs: llm.c's bf16 trainer, GPT-2 and llama2.cu.
Karpathy's GPT-2 trainer only runs on NVIDIA. Meta's Muse moved it to open SYCL, and it runs on NVIDIA, AMD and CPUs. And every step is proven.
Muse Port starts by reading the whole repository: llm.c, 22 CUDA files, 106 kernels.
Muse writes a plan, checked against that scan. Then it ports each item in an agent loop.
Nothing counts until a check the model never sees agrees. It even catches a one-term slip.
Here Muse ports GPT-2's training step. The check fails, Muse finds its own transpose mistake, fixes it, and all 10 steps match PyTorch.
The big test: llm.c's production trainer. Almost five thousand lines of bf16 CUDA, ported in one run, and llm.c's own test passes.
Then Muse tuned it on rented GPUs, in portable code. On mid-range NVIDIA cards, it takes about one and a half times CUDA's time. On an H100, 2.9 times. On AMD, 1,274 milliseconds a step, down to 63.
It ported 21 of llm.c's 22 kernel files. 20 pass their hidden check, and 19 also pass on NVIDIA against llm.c's own CUDA.
Put back together as llm.c-sycl, llm.c's own test prints: overall okay.
And a repo it had never seen, llama2.cu: ported in one run for 45 cents. The story matches, byte for byte, on CPU, NVIDIA and AMD.
Along the way, Muse's port hit a bug in oneMath, the open math library behind oneAPI. The fix is submitted upstream.
Every number is in a report built only from committed evidence, failures included.
The limits: the one-run trainer port worked one time in two. Kernels are fp32 at reduced sizes. And on an H100, portable code is still 2.9 times slower.
Moving AI off one vendor's GPUs, with proof. github.com/checocadena/museport.
